01

A photograph of nobody

With Realistic Vision V5.1 SD VAE ft-MSE YuNet

In

One text prompt per presenter: who they are, what they wear, where they are. Put this fragment in every presenter prompt: facing the camera, looking straight into the camera, lips closed. Example: RAW photo, television news anchor, woman in her mid 30s with long dark brown hair, red blazer, sitting at a news desk, facing the camera, looking straight into the camera, lips closed, calm expression, medium close-up, modern TV news studio, dark blue video walls blurred in background, broadcast footage, studio lighting.

Do

  1. Load the checkpoint with StableDiffusionPipeline, with its VAE replaced by sd-vae-ft-mse and the safety checker off. Run the UNet and the text encoder in bfloat16 and keep the VAE in float32.
  2. Use the DPM-Solver++ multistep sampler, order 2, Karras sigmas. Set algorithm_type="dpmsolver++" and solver_order=2 yourself. The checkpoint ships a DEIS sampler config, and without this the first run fails with final_sigmas_type zero is not supported for algorithm_type deis.
  3. Generate four candidates per presenter at 768 × 432, 25 steps, guidance 5.0, seeds 21 to 24. About 54 seconds an image.
  4. Put the candidates on a contact sheet and pick one. Reject: side views, a head that looks down or away, a tilted head, two people, the same face repeated, a hand beside the head, objects crossing the outline.
  5. Enlarge the pick with Lanczos to 1024 × 576. Then run image-to-image with the same prompt at strength 0.3 (6 of 20 steps), guidance 5, seed 1. About 50 seconds.
  6. Run YuNet on the result. Keep the eye centres, the mouth corners and the face box of the largest face. Compute iod.
  7. Refine the face. Crop a square of side 3.6 × iod (rounded to a multiple of 8), centred 0.45 × iod below the eye line. Scale it to 512 × 512. Run image-to-image at strength 0.35 (7 of 20 steps), guidance 5, seed 2, with the prompt RAW photo, close-up portrait of <description>, lips closed, looking at the camera, detailed skin texture, sharp focus. Paste it back through a feathered ellipse (radii 212 × 232 px of the 512 crop, blurred 16 px). Save as frame.png. The bulletin also passed the refined crop once through the VAE before pasting it. That served the inpainted mouths that were later dropped, so you can leave it out.
  8. The library's image-to-image pipelines assume one number format for the whole model. With a bfloat16 UNet and a float32 VAE they do not fit, so write the loop yourself. It is short. Use trailing timesteps round(linspace(1000, 0, steps + 1))[:-1] - 1, keep the last round(steps × strength) of them, add noise to the encoded image at the first one, apply classifier-free guidance, and take plain DDIM steps with no added noise.

The location stills are made the same way: one seed each, then the enlarging pass.

Out

frame.png per presenter. A small JSON file with the five landmark points, the face box and iod. One 1024 × 576 still per location.

Check

  • YuNet finds a face in frame.png (score threshold 0.5) and the largest one is your presenter. Print iod. The smallest face used here had 60.9 px between the eyes. Nothing smaller was tried.
  • Look at the picture. It should show one person, frontal, eyes on the camera, lips closed, with a clean outline against the background.
  • Read the log for a truncation warning. The text encoder reads 77 tokens. Two prompts here ran over and silently lost their last words.
  • Expect mismatches with the prompt. The reporter never got the microphone he was asked to hold.

Settings that worked

SettingValueWhat it means
Frame1024 × 576Every later picture, mask, field and map is in this frame
First size768 × 432Candidates are cheap at this size: about a minute each
SamplerDPM-Solver++ multistep, order 2, Karras sigmas, 25 steps, guidance 5.0Chosen over a 6-step LCM shortcut after a benchmark: 54 s against 22 s, kept for quality
Enlargestrength 0.3, 20 steps, guidance 5.0, seed 1Adds detail without changing the person
Face refinecrop 3.6 × iod, 0.45 × iod below the eye line, strength 0.35, seed 2A small face gets redrawn at 512 px
Negative promptcartoon, illustration, painting, drawing, 3d render, cgi, anime, doll, plastic skin, airbrushed, deformed, disfigured, extra fingers, bad hands, text, watermark, logo, caption, letters, subtitles, blurry face, cross-eyed, side view, profile, looking away, tilted head, nsfw, nudeThe last four pose terms were added after many of the first twenty candidates faced away
02

Cut the person out

With BiRefNet-portrait (ONNX, weights only)

In

frame.png. For the final cut-out and plate, the base frame from step 3.

Do

  1. Write the matting glue. Resize the picture to 1024 × 1024 (bilinear). Scale to 0 to 1. Normalise with mean (0.485, 0.456, 0.406) and standard deviation (0.229, 0.224, 0.225). Run the network. Take the first channel of its last output. If the values fall outside 0 to 1, apply a sigmoid. Resize back to the frame. Save as alpha.png. About 40 seconds an image.
  2. Run one image per process, with onnxruntime's CPU memory arena switched off (enable_cpu_mem_arena = False). A second image in the same process was killed for memory, twice.
  3. Make the cut-out from the base frame of step 3, so that it agrees with the pose renders:
    • Tighten the matte: alpha2 = clip((alpha - 0.25) / 0.7, 0, 1).
    • Replace the edge colours. Inpaint (OpenCV Telea, radius 4) every pixel where alpha2 <= 0.98, so that colours grow outwards from the solid interior. This removes the fringe of the old background.
    • Store colour plus alpha2. The bulletin used WebP at quality 88.
  4. Make the plate, the photograph with the person painted out:
    • The hole is every pixel where alpha is above 6 of 255, grown by an 11 × 11 ellipse. That keeps the real background up to five pixels from the outline.
    • Fill the hole with Telea inpainting, radius 7.
    • Soften the fill with depth into the hole. Blend towards a Gaussian blur of sigma 4 with weight clip((depth - 2) / 10, 0, 1). Then blend towards sigma 12 with weight clip((depth - 14) / 26, 0, 1).

Out

alpha.png, the cut-out (colour and transparency), the plate.

Check

  • Lay the cut-out over flat green and over a dark picture. Look at the hair. There should be no pale halo and no bright fringe of the old background.
  • Shift the cut-out 16 px sideways over the plate and look along the outline. The strip of plate that shows should read as out-of-focus background. It must not show a soft ghost of the head or a hard edge that follows the outline.
  • The matte should be white on the person, black elsewhere, and grey only in a thin band at the hair.

Settings that worked

SettingValueWhat it means
Matte input1024 × 1024The size this export of the network expects
Matte tightensubtract 0.25, divide by 0.7Drops the faint outer haze and makes the interior fully solid
Edge coloursTelea radius 4 where alpha2 <= 0.98Edge pixels take the person's colours, not the background's
Plate safety margin5 px (an 11 × 11 ellipse)Real background is kept right up to the person, because the body later moves 10 to 20 px
Plate softeningsigma 4 from 2 px in, sigma 12 from 14 px inThe strip a moving figure uncovers looks like blurred background, not streaks
03

Re-pose the face 65 times

With LivePortrait (ONNX export, weights only)

In

frame.png and the landmark points.

Do

Write the glue first. The model encodes a portrait once, describes the face by 21 keypoints in 3-D, and redraws the portrait for any new keypoints.

  1. Crop. A square of side 5.06 × iod. Its centre is 0.07 × iod from the midpoint of the eyes towards the mouth. Rotate it so that the line from the eyes to the mouth is vertical. Resample to 512 × 512, and to 256 × 256 for the two encoders. Keep the transform: every render goes back into the frame with it.
  2. Encode. appearance_feature_extractor.onnx (input img, 1×3×256×256, values 0 to 1) gives the appearance volume, 1×32×16×64×64. motion_extractor.onnx (same input) gives pitch, yaw, roll (66 bins each), t (3), exp (63), scale (1) and kp (63). An angle in degrees is sum(softmax(bins) × index) × 3 - 97.5.
  3. Keypoints. x = scale × (kp · R + exp), then add the x and y of t. R is the transpose of Rz · Ry · Rx built from pitch, yaw and roll. The source keypoints x_s use the values as read.
  4. Pose. Add offsets to exp (table below). For head poses add degrees to yaw or pitch. Compute the driving keypoints x_d the same way.
  5. Stitch. stitching.onnx (input input: x_s and x_d flattened, 126 numbers) returns 65 numbers. Add the first 63 to x_d. Add the last two to the x and y of every keypoint.
  6. Render. warping_spade.onnx (inputs feature_3d, kp_driving, kp_source) returns the image, 1×3×512×512, values 0 to 1. About 6.5 seconds a render.
  7. Leave out the head-pitch correction that the model's editing tools apply (they tilt the head back by 0.05° per jaw unit). Only the lower face is pasted into a fixed photograph here, so the upper face must stay put.

Offsets added to exp, per unit of each control. [k] is the keypoint, 0 to 20. They follow the sliders of the model's own editing tools. They were written from memory and then confirmed by rendering, so confirm them the same way.

ControlOffsets per unitValues used
aaa, jaw opens[19].y +0.001, [19].z +0.0001, [17].y −0.0001−8 (lips pressed) to 60, or 90 on one face
eee, lips spread[20].z −0.001, [20].y −0.001, [14].y −0.0013.5 and 7
woo, lips round and come forward[14].y +0.001, [3].y −0.0005, [7].y −0.0005, [17].z −0.00052 to 4 at rest, up to 15
smile[20].y −0.01, [14].y −0.02, [17].y +0.0065, [17].z +0.003, [13].y and [16].y −0.00275, [3].y and [7].y −0.0035−0.25 to −0.10 at rest, 0.38 for the broad smile
blink[11].y −0.001, [13].y +0.0003, [15].y −0.001, [16].y +0.0003−9 half closed, −17 closed
px, eyes sideways[11].x and [15].x: +0.0007 and +0.001 per unit when positive, +0.001 and +0.0007 when negative−7 and 7
py, eyes up or down[11].y −0.001, [15].y −0.001, and the brow control is reduced by py / 2−7 (down)
brow, positive[1].y +0.001, [2].y −0.00113
brow, negative[1].x −0.001, [2].x +0.001, [1].y +0.0003, [2].y −0.0003−12
headdegrees added to yaw or pitchyaw ±6.0, pitch ±5.0

Now render the pose set. Every photograph here smiles with closed lips. Poses built on that smile make the presenter talk through a held smile, lips stretched thin. So the neutral pose is a relaxed mouth: some of the smile taken out and the lips let a little forward. All speech poses are built on it.

PosesCountSettings, on top of the relaxed mouth unless noted
Relaxed mouth, the neutral pose1the face's rest settings only
The photograph's own expression1no offsets at all
Jaw, relaxed lips11aaa = 4, 8, 12, 16, 21, 26, 32, 38, 45, 52, 60
Lips half spread, fully spread8 + 8eee 3.5 and 7, each at aaa = 0, 5, 10, 16, 22, 30, 38, 48. Smile taken out, lips not pushed forward
Lips half rounded, fully rounded8 + 8woo = rest + 6 and rest + 12 (at most 15), at the same eight jaw values. Smile taken out
Smiling broadly8smile 0.38 with no rest settings, at the same eight jaw values
Lips pressed, for m, b, p1aaa −8
Lids2blink −9 and −17
Eyes left, right, down3px −7, px 7, py −7
Head turned, both ways2yaw +6.0 and −6.0
Head nodded, both ways2pitch +5.0 and −5.0
Brows raised, lowered2brow 13 and −12
Total657 to 14 minutes a face

Rest settings per face. To choose them, render a small grid first: rows are smile 0, −0.15, −0.3, and −0.2 with woo 3; columns are jaw 0, 16, 32, 48. Pick the row with fuller lips whose corners do not turn down.

Facesmile at rest (how far the smile is taken out)woo at rest (lips let forward)Jaw gain
Paige−0.1021
Cy−0.2031
Dee−0.2031
Sunny−0.2031
Mel−0.2541.5

Jaw gain multiplies every aaa value for that face. Mel's mouth opened about half as far as the others at the same setting, so his jaw list runs to 90 model units. At 90 he is still a believable open mouth. At 120 he shouts.

Then cut the regions:

  1. Put each render back into the frame with the crop transform. If the crop shrinks by more than 8 %, reduce it with area averaging first.
  2. Mouth mask. Over the 53 mouth poses, take the largest difference from the neutral render at each pixel (mean of the three channels). Keep pixels above 5 on a 0 to 255 scale. Keep only those inside an ellipse centred 1.25 × iod below the eye line with radii 1.35 × iod by 1.2 × iod, and at least 0.34 × iod below the eye line. Grow by 0.11 × iod, close the holes, and feather with a Gaussian of 0.05 × iod.
  3. Eye mask. The same from six eye poses: lids half and fully closed, eyes left, right and down, and the eyes of the closed-mouth broad smile. The ellipse is centred 0.05 × iod below the eye line with radii 1.2 × iod by 0.25 × iod. Grow by 0.06 × iod, feather 0.035 × iod. It must stop below the brows.
  4. Base frame. Inside both masks, replace the photograph by the neutral render. Now the still and every pose come from the same renderer, so a blend cannot show a seam.
  5. Store. Crop every pose to its mask's bounding box and store it opaque. Store each mask once.

Out

Per face: 65 renders at 512 × 512, the crop transform, the two jaw lists, the base frame, one mouth mask with 53 mouth poses, one eye mask with 6 eye poses.

Check

  • Render with no offsets and compare with the source crop. On the first face the mean absolute difference over the face was 5.57 on a 0 to 255 scale, and the render looked a touch softer.
  • Render jaw 60 and compare the eyes and forehead with the neutral render. Without the pitch correction the change was 1.10. With it, 19.71. If your upper face moves, the correction is still on.
  • Make a contact sheet of the poses and look at it. It should show the same person in every tile. The jaw row opens step by step. The pressed pose has the lips meeting. "ee" pulls the corners back without a grimace. "oo" is round. Half-closed lids are half closed, and closed lids are not squeezed. The head visibly turns each way.
  • Print the mask sizes. Mouth regions here were 168 to 314 px wide and 152 to 283 px tall. Eye regions were 134 to 273 px wide and 50 to 92 px tall. A mask that reaches into the hair or shoulders, or has stray blobs, is missing the ellipse.
  • Overlay the masks on the face. The eye mask must not touch the brows.

Jaw list, shaped rows0, 5, 10, 16, 22, 30, 38, 48The same idea for the spread, rounded and smiling rows

04

Record a voice and time every sound

With Phonon 31M (package ptts) Kokoro-82M (package kokoro) wav2vec 2.0 phoneme recogniser Whisper base

In

The script: for each line, who speaks, the text as shown in captions, and the text as spoken.

Do

  1. Respell for the speech model. Write names and abbreviations the way they should sound. Examples that were needed: "Sy DeCar", "A.I.", "U.S. east one", "D.N.S.", "five oh threes", "Why A Mel", "Yammel", "fin ops", "auto scaler", "re-tries", "ee-gress", "Dooty", "Tchilling". Keep the caption text separate.
  2. Record takes. Three takes of each line, seed 100 × line + take. With ptts: TTS(lang="en"), then synth(text, voice=..., seed=...). The cast was chosen from the publisher's written descriptions of its named voices: Harper, Miles, Easton, Juniper, Master Aldric. Write the takes as 32-bit float WAV. One take peaked at 1.05 and clipped when written as 16-bit. Phonon speaks about ten times faster than real time on this CPU.
  3. Check the words. Transcribe every take with Whisper. Lower-case both texts, strip punctuation, and map the recogniser's spellings of numbers and invented names onto the script's. Count wrong words by edit distance.
  4. Get the phoneme sequence of each line, with stress marks. Here Kokoro had read the same lines first, and its pipeline returns the phonemes it speaks, so those strings were used. Any text-to-phoneme tool will do. The engine in step 8 needs to know where m, b and p are, where the stressed vowels are, and where the pauses are.
  5. Forced alignment. Resample the take to 16 kHz. The recogniser gives a probability for each of its symbols every 20 ms. Its alphabet is finer than the script's, so list, for each script phoneme, the recogniser symbols that count as it, and add their probabilities. Examples: the vowel of "father" matches ɑː ɑ ɑːɹ ɒ a aː; r matches ɹ ɚ ɑːɹ ɔːɹ ɛɹ ɪɹ ʊɹ ɜː oːɹ aɪɚ; a flapped t matches ɾ t d. Then run a Viterbi search over the sequence blank, phoneme 1, blank, phoneme 2, and so on, letting two different phonemes touch. Place the boundary between two neighbours halfway between two estimates: the frame where the second becomes likelier than the first, and the midpoint between their certain frames. Time in seconds is frame × 0.02 + 0.0025.
  6. Clean up. Silence inside a phoneme's stretch is a pause, not sound. Pull the edges in to where there is signal (quiet means under 3.5 % of the 95th-percentile level, in 10 ms frames). A gap of 0.12 s or more that the script did not ask for becomes a pause of its own. A caption word appears with the first sound of its first spoken word.
  7. Choose the take with the fewest wrong words. Break ties by the take whose worst word matches its phonemes best.
  8. Level. Trim to 80 ms before the first sound and 180 ms after the last. Fade 15 ms in and 30 ms out. Measure loudness with ffmpeg's ebur128 filter and apply a plain gain to reach −19 LUFS. Round off the rare peak above 0.6 with a soft knee, 0.6 + 0.29 × tanh((x - 0.6) / 0.29), so nothing exceeds 0.89. Keep 24 kHz mono.
  9. Pitch. Track it with pYIN, 60 to 440 Hz, one value every 10 ms. Keep a value only inside a voiced phoneme, give or take 20 ms. Drop a value more than 10 semitones from the speaker's median, and one more than 4 semitones from the median of its neighbours. Store the median of each 40 ms in half semitones about the speaker's median.
  10. The 70 ms correction. If you take timing from a speech model's own report, test it against the audio first. Kokoro reports how many 25 ms frames each phoneme lasts. Adding those up gives each phoneme's start, and that sum runs late. Against the aligner, on Kokoro's own recordings, the model's phoneme starts were 73 ms late and its phoneme centres 62 ms late (median of 844 phonemes). The sound in each file also starts before the "first phoneme" time. The fix is a constant: move that model's phoneme times 0.07 s earlier. Times that come from the aligner get no shift. The voices in the video were timed by the aligner, so their shift is 0.

Out

Per line: the levelled recording, a list of phonemes with start, length and loudness, caption words with start times, and a pitch string.

Check

  • The Whisper transcript of every chosen take equals the script after normalising: 0 wrong words. Then transcribe the finished sound track too. Two mispronounced words here were only caught there.
  • Test the aligner on recordings whose timing is known. Here that test printed, for phoneme starts: aligner minus model −73 ms, scatter around that median 20 ms, 90 % within 55 ms. For centres: −62 ms, median 15 ms, 90 % within 47 ms. The constant is the model's lateness. The scatter is the aligner's own error and should stay under about one video frame.
  • Slide the mouth-opening curve of the finished animation against the loudness of the recording, in 10 ms steps up to 150 ms each way. With the late timing the best fit had the mouth 41 ms behind the voice. After the correction the mouth led by 14 ms, as real lips do. A mouth two frames behind its voice reads as dubbed, and no still frame shows it.
  • Every line has the same loudness and no sample above 0.89.
  • Plot one pitch string. Runs of exactly +12 semitones in hiss or silence, or a span of 27 semitones in one line, mean the three pitch filters are missing.

Settings that worked

SettingValueWhat it means
Takes3 per line, seed 100 × line + takeSpeech models slip: an added word, a dropped one, a name read another way
Timing shift, first speech model only−0.07 sIts reported sound times run about three of its 25 ms frames late against its own audio
Aligner hop0.02 sThe recogniser hears in 25 ms windows, 20 ms apart
Unscripted pause0.12 s or moreShorter gaps stay part of the neighbouring sounds
Trim0.08 s before, 0.18 s afterRoom for the fades without cutting a sound
Loudness−19 LUFS, soft knee at 0.6Scaling whole lines down to fit their peaks left one presenter 2 dB quieter
Pitch range60 to 440 Hz, frame 1536 and hop 240 samples at 24 kHzCovers all five voices
Pitch codeone character per 40 ms: chr(78 + round(2 × semitones)), limited to ±24, - where unvoicedBrows and head follow this contour
05

Ask a lip-sync network, then measure its answer

With Wav2Lip (ONNX, weights only) 2DFAN4 (ONNX, weights only)

In

The base frame, the mouth mask and the pose renders (step 3). The levelled recordings and phoneme times (step 4). The face box from YuNet.

Do

Hand-written rules for which sound opens the mouth how far were tried twice and looked wrong. So a network trained on real talking faces is asked instead. Its picture is 96 px across and soft, so it is measured and never shown.

  1. Wav2Lip glue, sound. Resample to 16 kHz. Pre-emphasis 0.97. STFT with n_fft 800, hop 200 (80 frames a second), window 800. 80 mel bands from 55 to 7600 Hz. Convert to decibels, 20 × log10(max(1e-5, S)) - 20, then scale with clip(8 × (dB + 100) / 100 - 4, -4, 4).
  2. Wav2Lip glue, face. Take the face box, with its height stretched by 4 % for chin room. Resize it to 96 × 96. The input target has six channels: the face with its lower half blacked out, then the whole face, values 0 to 1. The input source is 16 mel frames (0.2 s) shaped 1×80×16. The output is a 96 × 96 face. Paste it back into the frame at the box.
  3. Windowing. For picture i at 50 pictures a second, start the window at mel frame round(i × 80 / 50) - 6. That is 75 ms before the picture's own time. The stock code starts the window at the picture's time, and then every mouth is about a tenth of a second early.
  4. Landmark glue. Scale the face box so that its longer side is 195 px, centred in a 256 × 256 crop, values 0 to 1. 2DFAN4 returns 68 points on a 64-unit grid. Multiply by 4 and map back to the frame.
  5. Measure three numbers per picture, in units of iod: the opening (points 62 to 66, the inner lips), the outer lip height (points 51 to 57) and the mouth width (points 48 to 54).
  6. Calibrate each face. Make the same measurement on the base frame and on every mouth pose laid into the base frame through the mouth mask. First pass each through the same keyhole: shrink the face box to 96 × 96 and enlarge it again. Now you know which jaw value shows which opening on that face.
  7. Fix the timing. A "p" has a stretch of silence while the lips are closed. Find each p with a clear silence: at least 30 ms that is 28 dB or more below the recording's 90th-percentile level. Within 70 ms either side of the middle of that silence, find where the reference's opening is smallest. Take the median offset over all such sounds and move the reference by it.
  8. Put the faces on a common footing. For each presenter, over all samples inside speech sounds: "shut" is the 12th percentile of the opening, and the loud end is the 90th percentile minus shut. The gain is clip(0.155 / loud_end, 1.0, 2.2).
  9. Translate. Target opening = the face's own shut measurement + max(0, reading - shut) × gain. Look that opening up in the face's calibration to get a jaw value. Divide by 46 for the engine's opening. Above 0.9, halve the excess. For the lip shape, first subtract from the measured width the difference between the reference's width in long pauses and the face's own width at rest. Then compare it with the widths of the face's relaxed, fully spread and fully rounded rows at that jaw value: −1 is rounded, +1 is spread. Smooth both with a median of three and a 1-2-1 filter.
  10. Store the two curves per line, one value per 1/50 s.

It is slow: about 14 minutes on four cores for the bulletin's 4,320 samples.

Out

A calibration file (opening and width of every mouth pose of every face). Per line, a jaw curve from −0.12 to 1.3 and a lip-shape curve from −1 to 1, at 50 values a second.

Check

  • Print the calibration. The opening must rise with the jaw value on every face. Opening above shut, in units of iod, at jaw 16, 32 and 60:
FaceJaw 16Jaw 32Jaw 60Mouth width at rest
Paige0.0660.1290.2180.752
Cy0.0670.1330.2470.809
Dee0.0580.1220.2330.767
Sunny0.0610.1200.2220.812
Mel, with jaw gain 1.50.0390.1390.2880.739
  • Print the timing offset. Here the reference's lips were tightest 35 ms before the middle of the silence of a p (17 sounds, half of them between 48 and 18 ms early). It was moved 40 ms later, the nearest whole sample.
  • Average the reference's opening by kind of sound. Here: open vowels 0.54, mid vowels 0.39, close vowels 0.41, s z t d n 0.44, w and r 0.11 with rounded lips, m b p 0.04, f v 0.03. Lip sounds must come out near shut.
  • Print each line's typical and widest opening after translation. Here: typical 0.38 to 0.58, widest 0.83 to 1.10. If one presenter's mouth is shut for a third of their speech, "shut" was taken from the wrong place.
  • Draw the finished mouth frame by frame, every 1/20 s, each frame labelled with the sound being made. It should be shut on m, b and p, round on w and "oo", and open on "ah".

Settings that worked

SettingValueWhat it means
Rate50 measurements a second25 was used for voice sets that mattered less; it halves the work
Window start6 mel frames (75 ms) earlyRemoves most of the stock code's lead
Remaining shiftmeasured: 35 ms early, so moved 40 ms later; limited to ±80 msWhat is left after the window change. Measure it on your own recordings
"Shut"12th percentile of the opening while speakingThat is where the m, b and p readings lie. Pauses do not work: the network leaves the lips apart there
Loud end90th percentile above shutThe opening reached in clear, loud syllables
Common level0.155 × iodEvery presenter's loud end is brought to this: about a centimetre between the lips. A judgement, not a measurement
Gain limits1.0 to 2.2Nobody is scaled down. A timid reading is raised at most 2.2 times
Gains foundPaige 1.36, Cy 1.00, Dee 1.98, Sunny 2.05, Mel 1.33The network opens some faces far more timidly than others, whatever the voice
Jaw scale46 jaw units = an opening of 1The widest pose is 60, so the curve can reach 1.3
06

Turn two pictures into motion

With OpenCV DIS optical flow (no network)

In

The neutral render and six posed renders in frame coordinates: head turned each way, nodded each way, brows raised, brows lowered. alpha.png.

Do

Cross-fading between a head facing ahead and a head turned shows two faint heads. Optical flow between the two renders says where each point of the face goes instead.

  1. Compute dense optical flow (DIS, medium preset) from the neutral render to each posed render, in grey levels.
  2. Blur each field: Gaussian of 0.06 × iod for the four head fields, 0.03 × iod for the two brow fields.
  3. Weight the head fields so they fade to nothing before the edge of the model's crop and outside the person. Weight = (inside the crop, eroded with a square of side 0.25 × iod) × (matte above 0.1, grown with a 9 × 9 square), blurred by 0.12 × iod.
  4. Weight the brow fields with a band. It starts 0.13 × iod above the eye line, reaches full strength 0.12 × iod higher, and fades sideways and towards the hairline.
  5. Name the head fields by what they do on screen: which one carries the nose right, which one down. Do not trust the sign of the angle.
  6. Sample all six on a grid with a step of clip(round(0.11 × iod), 6, 14) px. Set the border of the grid to zero. Store each field as signed bytes with its own scale, 127 / largest value.

Out

Six displacement fields per face: right, left, down, up, brows up, brows down. Here the grids were 49 × 47 points at 10 px, 52 × 44 at 11, 53 × 49 at 12, 49 × 48 at 7 and 55 × 45 at 12, in 35 to 40 KB a face.

Check

  • Move the neutral render by the turn field and compare it with the real turned render. Here the mean difference left over was 2.6 to 5.0 grey levels, against 17 to 23 between the two renders.
  • Read the field at the nose. At 6° it moved 11 px on the smallest face and 21 px on the largest. The ears and hairline should barely move. Raised brows moved 2.8 to 7.2 px.
  • Draw the field as arrows over the face. They should all point one way, be longest at the nose, and vanish at the shoulders.

Settings that worked

SettingValueWhat it means
Head posesyaw ±6°, pitch ±5°The largest turn the fields are measured at. The bulletin stays within about 3.7°
Grid stepabout a ninth of iod, between 6 and 14 pxFine enough for the nose, small enough to store
Field storagesigned byte with a scale per fieldA first version stored eighths of a pixel and silently clipped at 15.9 px
Brow bandfrom 0.13 × iod above the eye lineBrows move; the eyes under them are left alone
07

Find the body and the loose hair

With BiSeNet face parser (ONNX, weights only)

In

frame.png, alpha.png, the landmark points.

Do

  1. Write the glue. A 512 × 512 crop, normalised with the same mean and standard deviation as in step 2, goes into input input. The output has 19 classes per pixel; take the largest. The labels used: 1 to 13 are the face, 14 and 15 the neck, 16 cloth, 17 hair.
  2. Run it twice per presenter. The network was trained on tight face crops, so use a tight crop of side 4.0 × iod, and a wide crop of the whole frame height (side at least 6.0 × iod). The wide one is what finds long hair lying on the chest. Trust the tight labels except along the crop's border.
  3. Find the chin: the lowest face pixel within 0.35 × iod of the face's centre column. Find where the clothes begin beside the neck: the 4th percentile of the heights of cloth pixels within 1.8 × iod of the centre. Do not look in the middle column. With an open neckline the cloth there starts a hand's width below the shoulders.
  4. Body map, 0 on the head and 1 on the torso. Face skin is 0. Cloth is 1. Everything else goes by height: a smooth ramp from 0.05 × iod above the chin or collar, whichever is higher, to 0.35 × iod below the lower of the two. Blur by 0.12 × iod inside the matte.
  5. Hair map, 0 on the scalp and 1 where hair is loose. For hair pixels take the larger of two values: "hang", a ramp from 0.25 to 1.75 × iod below the eye line, and "puff", 0.45 × how far the pixel stands outside a skull ellipse (full at 0.45 × iod). Multiply by 1 - 0.45 × body ramp, so that hair lying on the shoulders swings about half as far. Blur by 0.07 × iod.
  6. Wind map, only for a presenter outdoors. For hair pixels: more the further from the face (full at 0.5 × iod, never under 0.15), and most within 0.3 × iod of the outline. Blur by 0.06 × iod.
  7. Note four torso numbers: the shoulder line (0.5 × iod below where the clothes begin), the torso's middle, half the shoulder width, and the chin.
  8. Sample each map every 8 px: 129 × 73 values, one byte each.

Out

Per presenter: a body map, a hair map, a wind map where needed, and the four torso numbers.

Check

  • Draw the maps over the photograph: torso green, loose hair red, wind blue. The clothes should be green, the face clear, the neck graded. Red should appear only where hair hangs below the ears or stands away from the skull. Wind should sit on the outline of the hair.
  • Print the hair share. Here hair was 45 % of the first anchor's cut-out and more than half of it was loose; a bob was loose in its lower quarter; short hair and a bald head gave none.
  • Draw the shoulder line. It should cross the top of the shoulders, not the chest.

Settings that worked

SettingValueWhat it means
Map grid8 px, 129 × 73 valuesMovement is smooth, so a coarse map is enough
Two crops4.0 × iod and the frame heightOne crop size cannot label both the face and hair on the chest
Hair on the shouldersswings 0.55 as farIt bounced as freely as hair in the air before this
Wind floor0.15Even sheltered hair of an outdoor presenter stirs a little
08

Composite every frame, then record it

With no model plain JavaScript Canvas 2D and one small WebGL mesh headless Chromium ffmpeg

In

Everything from steps 1 to 7, bundled into one page as data: URIs: per presenter a plate, a cut-out, two masks, 53 mouth poses, 6 eye poses, six motion fields and the maps; and per line the recording, its timing, its pitch and its two lip curves. For the bulletin that came to 321 small images and sixteen recordings.

Do

Write the animation as a function of time. draw(t) paints the frame for show time t and keeps no state between frames, so any moment can be rendered directly. The one exception is the hair's spring, which starts afresh whenever the clock jumps.

One presenter, one frame:

  1. Work out the face for this moment: opening o, lip shape s, smile g, blink, gaze, brows, head turn, nod and tilt. Then the body: shift, tilt, lean, shoulder turn, breath, hair.
  2. Mouth. o × 46 picks two neighbouring jaw steps. s picks the relaxed row and the half or full row beside it: spread when s is positive, rounded when negative. So at most four poses are blended, plus the smile row. Below 0, blend in the pressed-lips pose, at full weight at −0.12. Start from the base frame's own pixels in a small canvas, add each pose with the opacity that leaves the exact weighted mix, cut the result to the mouth mask, and lay it on the cut-out.
  3. Eyes. The same with the eye poses: gaze, half and fully closed lids, and the smiling eyes.
  4. Mesh. Upload the composed cut-out as a texture. Draw it on a mesh whose points sit on the motion-field grid, continued over the whole frame. Each point carries the six displacements, a tilt weight and the three map values. The vertex shader adds: the weighted sum of the six fields; a tilt about the neck; the body's shift, tilt and lean; the breath lift; the shoulder turn; the hair's spring; the wind. Then it applies the pinning.
  5. Layers. Draw the plate. Draw anything that belongs between background and person. Draw the warped cut-out, scaled 1.2 % to 3.4 % more than the plate about the face. Add the camera move, film grain, a vignette, then captions and graphics on top.

What drives it:

  • Mouth. The two curves from step 5. In a pause the mouth comes to rest whatever the reference drew. A short press is added in each m, b and p so the lips truly meet.
  • Smile. A scale of three points: 0 is the relaxed mouth, used while speaking; 0.5 is the photograph's own expression, worn while listening; 1 is the broad smile, used where the script asks for one.
  • Brows and nods. Each stressed vowel gets a weight from its loudness, its pitch and its length. The strongest syllables carry a nod. The strongest high-pitched ones lift the brows.
  • Head. It resettles for every phrase, rides the pitch of the voice a little, and drifts slowly.
  • Blinks. At about half of the phrase ends, around glances, and at random in between.
  • Breath. In through the gap before each phrase, out while the phrase is spoken, quiet breathing between lines.
  • Body and hair. The torso shifts with some phrases, follows a head turn late, and dips into a stressed word. Loose hair hangs on a damped spring that follows the head.

Record:

  1. Open the page in headless Chromium with software WebGL: flags --use-gl=swiftshader and --enable-unsafe-swiftshader.
  2. For frame i from 0 to floor(length × 30) - 1, call draw(i / 30) and save the canvas as a JPEG at quality 0.92.
  3. If anything on screen shows the time of day, make the page's clock follow show time while rendering. Frames render several times slower than they play, and the clock in the first videos gained minutes.
  4. Build the sound track: each line's recording placed at its start time on the show's clock. The finished video used a recording of the page's own sound output instead, fitted to the timeline.
  5. Encode: ffmpeg -framerate 30 -i f%05d.jpg -i track.wav -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -crf 20 -c:a aac -b:a 128k -shortest -movflags +faststart out.mp4.

Out

The frames, then the MP4: 1024 × 576, 30 frames a second. Here 3,215 frames, 107.2 s.

Check

  • ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -show_entries stream=width,height,nb_frames -of csv=p=0 out.mp4 prints 1024,576,3215 for the bulletin. Yours prints your own frame count.
  • Force every kind of pose through the engine and put the results on one sheet. Look at each tile: turns, nods, tilt, brows, lids, gaze, smiles and the mouth grid, all on one unchanged face.
  • Smoothness. Render 100 frames at 60 a second and take the mean absolute difference between consecutive frames in the mouth region. Here: median 2.69, largest 5.26, against 2.78 for film grain alone in a still corner. No isolated jump.
  • Body. Render a presenter three ways: as shown, with the hair's spring and wind off, with body and hair off. Optical flow between matching frames is what each part adds. Here it agreed with what the engine asked for to about 0.1 px on the body and 0.25 px on hair. Shoulders rose and fell over 4.6 to 6.9 px. The body carried the head 11 to 21 px sideways.
  • The figure never lifts off the bottom edge. Count how much of the bottom row it covers: here 99.7 % to 102.3 % of what it covers when still. Optical flow is not reliable in the last rows of a picture.
  • Count events over the whole bulletin. Here, on the build before body and hair were added: 58 lip presses, 61 nods, 28 brow lifts, 18 blinks a minute by whoever is speaking. First settings gave 31 blinks a minute and five or six brow lifts in nine seconds, which is too much.
  • Sound against picture. Find each line's recording in the video's sound track by correlation. On the first video with sound, each voice sat within −1 to +8 ms of its place.
  • A frame took about 25 ms to draw in software rendering.

Settings that worked

The mouth and face:

SettingValueWhat it means
Track sampling120 a secondMouth tracks are sampled this often and smoothed forwards and backwards
Smoothingjaw 0.010 s, lip shape 0.025 s, lip press 0.005 sTime constants. Nothing moves faster than a face can
Opening range−0.12 to 1.3Below 0 the lips are pressed. 1 is 46 jaw units
Smile scale0, 0.5, 1Relaxed while speaking; the photograph's own expression while listening; a broad smile
Smile releaselets go 0.45 to 0.15 s before the first sound, returns 0.35 to 1.1 s after the lastA smile is something that happens, not something worn while talking
Smile and roundingsmile × (1 − 0.6 × rounding)Lips cannot round and smile at once
Smiling eyesonly above 0.5The eyes join in for a smile broader than the photograph's own
Lip press, mstarts 12 % into the sound; ends at 85 % of it, or 0.12 s after it starts if that is soonerA short press in the middle
Lip press, p and bends 25 ms before the end of the sound, lasts up to 70 msJust before the release. A press in the middle of a p after a pause shut the mouth a fifth of a second early
Lip press, limitsat least 40 ms; 30 to 90 ms in, 30 to 70 ms outSlower where the mouth is still open. Long ramps swallowed short vowels
Pausesopening × 0.1 in a pause over 0.5 s, × 0.4 in a shorter oneThe reference tends to leave the lips apart
Breath before speakingopening 0.07, from 0.3 s to 0.07 s before the first soundLips part slightly, as for a breath
Lead-in0.28 s by default; 0.22 to 0.95 s per lineListening time before a voice starts. The longest is a satellite delay
Tail0.26 sA line ends this long after its recording
Blink0.27 s: 65 ms to close, 40 ms shut, 165 ms to openPasses through the half-closed pose
Blink spacingnone within 0.9 s of another, none in the last 0.5 s of a lineA cut once landed on closed eyes
Random blinksslots of 1.25 s, 1 in 5 has a blink, 14 % of those are doubleKeeps the rhythm irregular
Eye dartsa small jump about every 0.85 sEyes are never quite still
Nodweight 0.45 or more, and the strongest within 0.45 sOnly syllables that stand out
Brow liftweight 0.7 or more, pitch 1.5 semitones or more above the median, 1.3 s apart, strength 0.3 to 0.65More than this looks like mugging
Head limitsturn within ±1 field (6°), nod −0.9 to 1 field (5°), brows up to 0.92Never beyond what was measured

The body, the hair and the picture:

SettingValueWhat it means
Pinning0.5 × iod up from the bottom edge, 0.45 × iod in from each sideUp-and-down movement fades to nothing at the bottom, sideways movement at the sides. A band 0.9 × iod tall held the shoulders still
Tiltfull at the face, none 3.3 × iod away, about a point 1.6 × iod below the face centreThe head tilts about the neck and the shoulders stay
Breath lift0.11 × iod for a whole breath; the head takes a quarterAbout 7 mm on a real person
Breath widening0.7 %The chest widens as it fills
Breath timingin ends 40 ms before the first sound; in for clamp(0.8 × gap, 0.14, 0.6) s; out at 0.1 a second of speech; between lines in for 1.5 s, out for 2.4 sA short gap allows only a quick top-up
Body resettleson 45 % of phrases, 0.02 to 0.07 × iod, over 1.1 s (the head takes 0.55 s)Resettling on every phrase rocked the body from side to side
Shoulders follow the headsmoothed over 0.3 s; shift 0.03 × iod per unit of head turnThey take up a look to the side, not a quick nod
Stress dip0.022 × iod down and 0.8 % lean, 0.12 s behind the nodTwice this bounced the shoulders on every stressed word
Shoulder turn0.1 × iod at the middle of the chest; 0.35 of it at the shoulder line, all of it 1.4 × iod belowThe outline hardly moves and the collar stays under the neck
SwayPaige 1, Cy 0.75, Dee 2, Sunny 1.8, Mel 0.9More for the two who stand
Hair spring, cycles a secondPaige 1.8, Cy 4, Dee 3.4, Sunny 2.4Long hair is slow, curls are fast
Hair spring, dampingPaige 0.32, Cy 0.5, Dee 0.42, Sunny 0.38How soon the swing dies
Hair swingPaige 1.6, Cy 0.8, Dee 1.1, Sunny 1.5, Mel 0How far loose hair trails the head
Hair limitsat most 0.14 × iod; up-and-down is 0.6 of sideways; stepped every 4 ms; restarts when the clock jumps by more than 0.25 sKeeps the spring stable through cuts and seeks

no

lim

What it cannot do

  • It is a warp of one photograph per person. A turned shoulder shows no new side of a jacket. Cloth does not crease. Hair does not part. Hands never come into view.
  • Heads turn about six degrees at most. The motion fields are measured at 6° and 5°, and the bulletin stays within about 3.7°. A glance to the side is mostly eyes.
  • There is no pose for the lower lip against the upper teeth. f and v are drawn as a nearly shut mouth.
  • Teeth and tongue are whatever the re-posing model drew for each jaw opening.
  • The lip reference is a network's opinion. Its mouths are soft and it tends to under-open. The common level of 0.155 is a judgement.
  • The strip of plate that a moving figure uncovers is a softened guess, not what was behind the person.
  • The voices read evenly. They do not act, and they have no breaths. English only.
  • Nobody watched or listened during the build. Amounts of movement were set from how far real bodies move and from still frames. If the body reads as too still or too busy, change the sway values and the factors in the body's settings.
  • Only headless Chromium with software rendering was run. No phone, no GPU, no other browser.
  • Backgrounds are still photographs with a camera move on top.
